Gregory I. Reigning from 590 to 604, Gregory was a transformative pope who bridged the transition from the classical Roman world to the medieval Catholic Church. As the first monk to ascend the papal throne, he established the papacy as a dominant temporal power in Italy while dramatically expanding its spiritual influence across Western Europe. Through his prolific writings, administrative reforms, and missionary efforts, he earned the title of Doctor of the Church and became the second pope known as the Great.

In 597, Gregory dispatched the Gregorian mission led by Augustine of Canterbury to convert the pagan Anglo-Saxons of England, initiating the Christianization of the British Isles. He successfully negotiated peace treaties and military defense against the invading Lombards, effectively stepping into the civil leadership vacuum left by the Byzantine Empire. He standardized the administration of the Patrimony of St. Peter, the papal estates, using agricultural revenues to feed refugees, fund hospitals, and ransom captives in plague-ravaged Rome. He adopted the humble title Servus servorum Dei—Servant of the servants of God—to counter the claims of the Patriarch of Constantinople, a title that popes continue to use to this day.

Gregory codified liturgical reforms and patronized plainsong, lending his name to Gregorian chant, which became the dominant musical tradition of medieval Europe. He authored the Pastoral Care, a foundational handbook on spiritual leadership and governance that remained mandatory reading for bishops for centuries. His Dialogues, a collection of four books detailing the miracles and lives of Italian saints, became widely popular and served as the primary biography of Saint Benedict of Nursia. He also wrote the Moralia in Job, an exhaustive commentary on the Book of Job that shaped medieval moral theology and allegorical biblical interpretation.
